Contents of https://www.nuget.org/packages/Markout/: **Markup adds instructions to content. Markout removes structure from data.** Markout is a source-generated .NET serializer that projects objects into structured, human-readable documents. You annotate your models with attributes that describe data relationships — identity, enumeration, tabulation, measurement, hierarchy — and the source generator emits code that writes through an abstract renderer. The same object graph produces Markdown tables, ANSI terminal output with colored bars, plain text with aligned columns, pretty tables, or TSV rows, without the developer making visual decisions. ### Quick Start ``` using Markout; var artist = new Artist( Name: "Sarah McLachlan", Genre: "Pop / Adult Contemporary", Origin: "Halifax, Nova Scotia", DebutYear: 1988, BestKnownFor: "Angel, Building a Mystery, Adia"); MarkoutSerializer.Serialize(artist, Console.Out, ArtistContext.Default); [MarkoutSerializable(TitleProperty = nameof(Artist.Name))] public record Artist( string Name, string Genre, string Origin, int DebutYear, string BestKnownFor); [MarkoutContext(typeof(Artist))] public partial class ArtistContext : MarkoutSerializerContext { } ``` **Output:** ``` # Sarah McLachlan | Field | Value | | ----- | ----- | | Genre | Pop / Adult Contemporary | | Origin | Halifax, Nova Scotia | | Debut Year | 1988 | | Best Known For | Angel, Building a Mystery, Adia | ``` Three things: a record, a context, one line of serialization. Package `Markout` (the source generator ships in it — no extra package). Default output is

## The required pattern (3 parts — all mandatory)

```csharp
using Markout;

// 1. Annotate every model type. List<T> -> table, scalar -> field.
[MarkoutSerializable(TitleProperty = nameof(Title))]   // TitleProperty -> the H1 heading
public class Report
{
    public string Title { get; set; } = "";
    public int Count { get; set; }                     // scalar -> "Count | 3" field row
    [MarkoutSection(Name = "Items")]                   // -> "## Items" heading
    public List<Row>? Items { get; set; }              // List<T> -> a table
}

[MarkoutSerializable]
public class Row { public string Name { get; set; } = ""; public string Value { get; set; } = ""; }

// 2. Register EVERY type on a partial context (the source generator fills it in).
[MarkoutContext(typeof(Report))]
[MarkoutContext(typeof(Row))]
public partial class ReportContext : MarkoutSerializerContext { }

// 3. Serialize THROUGH the context.
MarkoutSerializer.Serialize(report, Console.Out, ReportContext.Default);
```

## Scalar field shaping (title, description, per-value formatting)

Shape scalar properties with attributes — never pre-format strings in the model or hand-write rows:

```csharp
[MarkoutSerializable(
    TitleProperty = nameof(Name),               // -> the H1 heading
    DescriptionProperty = nameof(Summary),      // -> a paragraph under the H1 (NOT a Field | Value row)
    FieldLayout = FieldLayout.Inline)]          // Table (default) | Inline | Bulleted | Numbered | Plain
public class Component
{
    public string Name { get; set; } = "";
    public string Summary { get; set; } = "";

    [MarkoutDisplayFormat("{0:N0} downloads")]  // 5100000 -> "5,100,000 downloads"
    public long Downloads { get; set; }

    [MarkoutDisplayFormat("{0:yyyy-MM-dd}")]    // DateTime -> "2024-06-01"
    public DateTime Published { get; set; }

    [MarkoutBoolFormat("Yes", "No")]            // true -> "Yes", false -> "No"
    public bool Verified { get; set; }
}
```

- `DescriptionProperty` renders a property as a description paragraph, not a table row.
- `FieldLayout.Inline` puts the scalar fields on one line (`Owner: … | Status: …`) instead of a table.
- `[MarkoutDisplayFormat("{0:…}")]` / `[MarkoutBoolFormat(t,f)]` format a value **in place** — do not bake
  the formatting into the getter or build the cell string yourself.

## Gotchas (where System.Text.Json intuition is wrong)

- **No reflection fallback.** There is no `Serialize(obj)` overload. EVERY `Serialize` call takes a
  `MarkoutSerializerContext`. Omitting it does not compile — the #1 mistake.
- **Register every type.** A model missing `[MarkoutSerializable]` + `[MarkoutContext(typeof(T))]`
  won't serialize. The context class MUST be `partial`.
- **Markout attributes, not Json:** `[MarkoutSerializable]` (not `[JsonSerializable]`),
  `[MarkoutContext]`, `[MarkoutSection(Name=...)]`, `[MarkoutPropertyName]`, `[MarkoutIgnore]`.
- **Type drives rendering, not markup:** `List<T>` -> table; scalar -> `Field | Value` row;
  `[MarkoutSection(Name="X")]` -> a `## X` heading above the property.
- **`[MarkoutIgnoreInTable]` on non-tabular list properties** (`List<Metric>`, `List<Breakdown>`,
  `List<TreeNode>`, `List<Description>`, `Callout`) or they get mistreated as table columns.

Real CLIs expose `-v`/`--detail`/`--quiet` and section selectors. The anti-pattern is a separate
render path (or DTO) per level. With Markout you keep **one model** and select what renders — and,
importantly, drive **what you collect** from the requested verbosity so you don't over-scan.

## Compact summary via field layout

`AutoFields` renders scalar properties as fields; tune the summary without new types:

```csharp
[MarkoutSerializable(
    TitleProperty = nameof(Name),
    FieldLayout = FieldLayout.Inline)]   // Table (default) | Inline | Bulleted | Numbered | Plain
public class View
{
    public string Name { get; set; } = "";
    [MarkoutSkipNull] public string? Summary { get; set; }   // drops out of the terse view when null
}
```

`FieldLayout.Inline` gives a pipe-separated one-liner header; `Table` gives a two-column field block.
Choose the terse shape for quiet mode, the fuller sections for detail.

## Verbosity as section selection

Verbosity is a caller concept. Express it as the set of sections to render:

```csharp
static readonly string[] QuietSections  = { "Summary" };
static readonly string[] DetailSections = { "Summary", "Members", "Diagnostics", "Sources" };

var sections = verbose ? DetailSections : QuietSections;
var options = new MarkoutWriterOptions { IncludeSections = new HashSet<string>(sections) };
MarkoutSerializer.Serialize(view, Console.Out, new MarkdownFormatter(), ctx, options);
```

The higher-value workflow: let the requested sections **promote** how much data you gather, so a
narrow request stays cheap and a `--section Diagnostics` request pulls exactly the data it needs.
Verbosity is **your** concept — `MarkoutWriterOptions` has no `Verbosity` property. Keep the policy
in your collection code; Markout only ever sees the populated model + `IncludeSections`.

enum Verbosity { Quiet, Normal, Detailed }

Verbosity required = GetRequiredVerbosity(requestedSections);          // e.g. Diagnostics => Detailed
var verbosity = (Verbosity)Math.Max((int)cliVerbosity, (int)required);
var model = Collect(verbosity);                                        // scan only as deep as needed

var options = new MarkoutWriterOptions { IncludeSections = new HashSet<string>(sections) };
MarkoutSerializer.Serialize(model, Console.Out, new MarkdownFormatter(), ctx, options);
```

Markout renders whatever the model carries; the verbosity policy is expressed to it purely through
which properties you populate + `IncludeSections`. This is the pattern behind tools that map
`-D`/`-S` flags to a single reusable view.

- One model, many levels — do not fork a `RenderQuiet` / `RenderFull` pair of string builders.
- Keep the section-name constants in one place; reuse them for both collection and `IncludeSections`.

# Markout **Markup adds instructions to content. Markout removes structure from data.** Markout is a source-generated .NET serializer that projects objects into structured, human-readable documents. You annotate your models with attributes that describe data relationships — identity, enumeration, tabulation, measurement, hierarchy — and the source generator emits code that writes through an abstract renderer. The same object graph produces Markdown tables, ANSI terminal output with colored bars, plain text with aligned columns, pretty tables, or TSV rows, without the developer making visual decisions. ## Quick Start ```csharp using Markout; var artist = new Artist( Name: "Sarah McLachlan", Genre: "Pop / Adult Contemporary", Origin: "Halifax, Nova Scotia", DebutYear: 1988, BestKnownFor: "Angel, Building a Mystery, Adia"); MarkoutSerializer.Serialize(artist, Console.Out, ArtistContext.Default); [MarkoutSerializable(TitleProperty = nameof(Artist.Name))] public record Artist( string Name, string Genre, string Origin, int DebutYear, string BestKnownFor); [MarkoutContext(typeof(Artist))] public partial class ArtistContext : MarkoutSerializerContext { } ``` **Output:** ```markdown # Sarah McLachlan | Field | Value | | ----- | ----- | | Genre | Pop / Adult Contemporary | | Origin | Halifax, Nova Scotia | | Debut Year | 1988 | | Best Known For | Angel, Building a Mystery, Adia | ``` Three things: a record, a context, one line of serialization. The `TitleProperty` becomes a heading; everything else renders as a field table. ## Field Layouts The same model renders differently with `FieldLayout`. The default is a two-column table. Switch to `Inline` for a compact summary line: ```csharp [MarkoutSerializable(TitleProperty = nameof(Artist.Name), FieldLayout = FieldLayout.Inline)] public record Artist( ... ); ``` ```markdown # Sarah McLachlan Genre: Pop / Adult Contemporary | Origin: Halifax, Nova Scotia | Debut Year: 1988 | Best Known For: Angel, Building a Mystery, Adia ``` Or `Bulleted` for a list: ```csharp [MarkoutSerializable(TitleProperty = nameof(Artist.Name), FieldLayout = FieldLayout.Bulleted)] public record Artist( ... ); ``` ```markdown # Sarah McLachlan - Genre: Pop / Adult Contemporary - Origin: Halifax, Nova Scotia - Debut Year: 1988 - Best Known For: Angel, Building a Mystery, Adia ``` Or `Numbered`: ```markdown # Sarah McLachlan 1. Genre: Pop / Adult Contemporary 2. Origin: Halifax, Nova Scotia 3. Debut Year: 1988 4. Best Known For: Angel, Building a Mystery, Adia ``` Or `Plain` — bare lines, no markers. Each line ends with two trailing spaces, which is the markdown signal for `
`: ```markdown # Sarah McLachlan Genre: Pop / Adult Contemporary Origin: Halifax, Nova Scotia Debut Year: 1988 Best Known For: Angel, Building a Mystery, Adia ``` The data model doesn't change — only the attribute controls the shape. ## Adding Sections and Tables Add `[MarkoutSection]` to group properties with headings, and use `List` for tables: ```csharp [MarkoutSerializable(TitleProperty = nameof(Title))] public class CityReport { public string Title { get; set; } = ""; public string Province { get; set; } = ""; public int Population { get; set; } [MarkoutSection(Name = "Landmarks")] public List? Languages { get; set; } [MarkoutSection(Name = "Top Contributors")] [MarkoutIgnoreInTable] public List? TopContributors { get; set; } [MarkoutSection(Name = "Releases")] public List? Releases { get; set; } } ``` Run it: ```bash dotnet run samples/GitHubRepo/GitHubRepo.cs # ANSI terminal (default) dotnet run samples/GitHubRepo/GitHubRepo.cs -- dotnet/runtime --format markdown # Markdown dotnet run samples/GitHubRepo/GitHubRepo.cs -- dotnet/runtime --format table # Compact table dotnet run samples/GitHubRepo/GitHubRepo.cs -- dotnet/runtime --format tsv # Stable TSV rows dotnet run samples/GitHubRepo/GitHubRepo.cs -- dotnet/runtime --format jsonl # Stable JSONL rows ``` **Markdown output** for `dotnet/runtime`: ```markdown # dotnet/runtime .NET is a cross-platform runtime for cloud, mobile, desktop, and IoT apps. | Field | Value | | ----- | ----- | | Stars | 17,703 | | Forks | 5,353 | | Open Issues | 8,371 | | Language | C# | | License | MIT License | ## Languages | Category | Count | % | | -------- | ----- | - | | C# | 80 | 83 | | C++ | 9 | 9 | | C | 7 | 7 | ## Top Contributors | Label | Value | | ----- | ----- | | vargaz | 11910 | | stephentoub | 10418 | | kumpera | 4074 | | jkotas | 3245 | ## Releases | Tag | Name | Published | | --- | ---- | --------- | | v8.0.24 | .NET 8.0.24 | 2026-02-10 | | v9.0.13 | v9.0.13 | 2026-02-10 | | v10.0.3 | .NET 10.0.3 | 2026-02-10 | ``` **Table output** — same model, `--format table`: ```text FIELD VALUE Stars 17,703 Forks 5,353 Open Issues 8,371 Language C# License MIT License TAG NAME PUBLISHED v8.0.24 .NET 8.0.24 2026-02-10 v9.0.13 v9.0.13 2026-02-10 v10.0.3 .NET 10.0.3 2026-02-10 ``` **JSONL output** — same table projection, `--format jsonl`: ```jsonl {"tag":"v8.0.24","name":".NET 8.0.24","published":"2026-02-10"} {"tag":"v9.0.13","name":"v9.0.13","published":"2026-02-10"} {"tag":"v10.0.3","name":".NET 10.0.3","published":"2026-02-10"} ``` The pattern is always the same: deserialize your API data, project to a model, serialize. Renderers decide how to present each shape. | Relationship | C# type | What it means | Markdown | ANSI | |---|---|---|---|---| | **Identity** | `string`, `int`, `bool` | Named value | `Key: value` | Bold key, value | | **Enumeration** | `string[]` | Sequence of items | `- item` | Bullet list | | **Tabulation** | `List` | Uniform records | `\| col \| col \|` | Space-padded table | | **Section** | `[MarkoutSection]` | Logical grouping | `## Heading` | Colored heading | | **Description** | `List` | Terms with explanations | `- **Term:** text` | Bold term, text | | **Measurement** | `List` | Comparative quantities | `Label ████░░ 45` | Colored bars | | **Composition** | `List` | Parts of a whole | `██▓▓▒░` stacked | Colored segments | | **Hierarchy** | `List` | Parent-child structure | `├── node` | Box-drawing tree | | **Quotation** | `CodeSection` | Verbatim content | ` ```code``` ` | Syntax display | | **Attention** | `Callout` | Important messages | `> [!WARNING]` | Colored label | Plus structural shapes: **Quotation** (prose quotation), **Matrix** (2D pivot grid), **Rule** (section separator). ### Record Types Shapes that need structured input provide record types named for what the data *is*, not what it *looks like*: ```csharp new Metric("Build Time", 4.2) // measurement new Description("dotnet-inspect", "API surface inspection tool") // term + explanation new Breakdown("Jan 2025", [new("Critical", 1), new("High", 3)]) // proportional composition new Callout(CalloutSeverity.Warning, "3 vulnerabilities found") // attention new CodeSection("csharp", "public class Foo { }") // verbatim content ``` ## Renderers Markout ships five formatters. The serializer writes through `MarkoutWriter` (the orchestrator) — swap the formatter, change the output. | Formatter | Output | Use case | |---|---|---| | **MarkdownFormatter** | GitHub-Flavored Markdown | Documentation, LLM tool output, rendered reports | | **PlainTextFormatter** | Plain text without markup | Minimal output, no syntax characters | | **UnicodeFormatter** | Box-drawing characters | Rich tables with borders, no color | | **TableFormatter** | Tables, lists, fields | Compact summaries, pretty tables, TSV/JSONL rows | | **DiagramFormatter** | Trees and structural diagrams | Dependency graphs, file trees | Optional packages: | Package | Formatter | Use case | |---|---|---| | **Markout.Ansi.Spectre** | `SpectreFormatter` | Rich terminal UI via Spectre.Console | Formatters declare which shapes they support by implementing capability interfaces (`ITableFormatter`, `IFieldFormatter`, `ITreeFormatter`, etc.). Unsupported shapes are silently skipped — the data is never lost, only the visual sophistication changes. ### Format promises - Markdown table-cell and heading text is treated as literal data: the structural characters `&`, `<`, `>`, and backtick are escaped to entities (`&`, `<`, `>`, ```) so the value renders verbatim rather than being interpreted as HTML or a code span. Table cells additionally normalize the delimiting pipe to `|`. - The exception is content inside a rendered `` span, where those characters are literal: there, a pipe is escaped as `\|` (GFM unescapes it while splitting table rows, before code-span parsing) and angle brackets/ampersands need no escaping. - Semantic inline `...` tags render as Markdown code spans and as plain text in table, TSV, and JSONL output. - `TableFormatter` with `MarkoutTableMode.Tsv` uses stable snake_case headers by default and never emits embedded tabs or newlines in table cells. - `TableFormatter` with `MarkoutTableMode.Jsonl` uses stable snake_case property names by default and emits one JSON object per table row. - `TableFormatter` with `MarkoutTableMode.Pretty` renders the same projection as TSV, with each column starting at a uniform position across rows. ## Templates Templates let you author document structure in Markdown and fill data slots at runtime. The same template renders to any format — Markdown, plain text, or ANSI terminal. **template.md:** ```markdown # .NET Security Report for {{date}} The following vulnerabilities were disclosed this month. {{vuln-table}} | Level | CVSS Range | Response | | ----- | ---------- | -------- | | Critical | 9.0–10.0 | Patch immediately | | High | 7.0–8.9 | Patch within 30 days | {{#if commits}} ## Commits {{commit-table}} {{/if}} ``` **Program.cs:** ```csharp using Markout; using Markout.Templates; var template = MarkoutTemplate.Load("template.md"); template.TableOptions = new TableFormatterOptions(); // smooth column widths template.Bind("date", "February 2026"); template.Bind("vuln-table", vulnerabilityData); // IMarkoutFormattable template.Bind("commits", hasCommits ? # Multi-view & verbosity — summary/detail from one model

Real CLIs expose `-v`/`--detail`/`--quiet` and section selectors. The anti-pattern is a separate
render path (or DTO) per level. With Markout you keep **one model** and select what renders — and,
importantly, drive **what you collect** from the requested verbosity so you don't over-scan.

## Compact summary via field layout

`AutoFields` renders scalar properties as fields; tune the summary without new types:

```csharp
[MarkoutSerializable(
    TitleProperty = nameof(Name),
    FieldLayout = FieldLayout.Inline)]   // Table (default) | Inline | Bulleted | Numbered | Plain
public class View
{
    public string Name { get; set; } = "";
    [MarkoutSkipNull] public string? Summary { get; set; }   // drops out of the terse view when null
}
```

`FieldLayout.Inline` gives a pipe-separated one-liner header; `Table` gives a two-column field block.
Choose the terse shape for quiet mode, the fuller sections for detail.

## Verbosity as section selection

Verbosity is a caller concept. Express it as the set of sections to render:

```csharp
static readonly string[] QuietSections  = { "Summary" };
static readonly string[] DetailSections = { "Summary", "Members", "Diagnostics", "Sources" };

var sections = verbose ? DetailSections : QuietSections;
var options = new MarkoutWriterOptions { IncludeSections = new HashSet<string>(sections) };
MarkoutSerializer.Serialize(view, Console.Out, new MarkdownFormatter(), ctx, options);
```

Combine with same-name section variants (see conditional-composition) when a level needs a *different
projection* of a section rather than just its presence.

## Verbosity backpressure — collect only what's rendered

The higher-value workflow: let the requested sections **promote** how much data you gather, so a
narrow request stays cheap and a `--section Diagnostics` request pulls exactly the data it needs.
Verbosity is **your** concept — `MarkoutWriterOptions` has no `Verbosity` property. Keep the policy
in your collection code; Markout only ever sees the populated model + `IncludeSections`.

```csharp
enum Verbosity { Quiet, Normal, Detailed }

// Resolve requested sections first, then raise your own verbosity to satisfy them, THEN collect.
Verbosity required = GetRequiredVerbosity(requestedSections);          // e.g. Diagnostics => Detailed
var verbosity = (Verbosity)Math.Max((int)cliVerbosity, (int)required);
var model = Collect(verbosity);                                        // scan only as deep as needed

var options = new MarkoutWriterOptions { IncludeSections = new HashSet<string>(sections) };
MarkoutSerializer.Serialize(model, Console.Out, new MarkdownFormatter(), ctx, options);
```

Markout renders whatever the model carries; the verbosity policy is expressed to it purely through
which properties you populate + `IncludeSections`. This is the pattern behind tools that map
`-D`/`-S` flags to a single reusable view.

## The required pattern (3 parts — all mandatory)

```csharp
using Markout;

// 1. Annotate every model type. List<T> -> table, scalar -> field.
[MarkoutSerializable(TitleProperty = nameof(Title))]   // TitleProperty -> the H1 heading
public class Report
{
    public string Title { get; set; } = "";
    public int Count { get; set; }                     // scalar -> "Count | 3" field row
    [MarkoutSection(Name = "Items")]                   // -> "## Items" heading
    public List<Row>? Items { get; set; }              // List<T> -> a table
}

[MarkoutSerializable]
public class Row { public string Name { get; set; } = ""; public string Value { get; set; } = ""; }

// 2. Register EVERY type on a partial context (the source generator fills it in).
[MarkoutContext(typeof(Report))]
[MarkoutContext(typeof(Row))]
public partial class ReportContext : MarkoutSerializerContext { }

// 3. Serialize THROUGH the context.
MarkoutSerializer.Serialize(report, Console.Out, ReportContext.Default);
```

Shape scalar properties with attributes — never pre-format strings in the model or hand-write rows:

```csharp
[MarkoutSerializable(
    TitleProperty = nameof(Name),               // -> the H1 heading
    DescriptionProperty = nameof(Summary),      // -> a paragraph under the H1 (NOT a Field | Value row)
    FieldLayout = FieldLayout.Inline)]          // Table (default) | Inline | Bulleted | Numbered | Plain
public class Component
{
    public string Name { get; set; } = "";
    public string Summary { get; set; } = "";

    [MarkoutDisplayFormat("{0:N0} downloads")]  // 5100000 -> "5,100,000 downloads"
    public long Downloads { get; set; }

    [MarkoutDisplayFormat("{0:yyyy-MM-dd}")]    // DateTime -> "2024-06-01"
    public DateTime Published { get; set; }

    [MarkoutBoolFormat("Yes", "No")]            // true -> "Yes", false -> "No"
    public bool Verified { get; set; }
}
```

- `[MarkoutDisplayFormat("{0:…}")]` / `[MarkoutBoolFormat(t,f)]` format a value **in place** — do not bake

12. # Markout — produce Markdown/structured output from objects
13. 
14. Source-generated serializer. Default output is Markdown. Package `Markout` (includes the

18. 
19. ```csharp
20. using Markout;
21. 
22. // 1. Annotate every model type. List<T> -> table, scalar -> field.
23. [MarkoutSerializable(TitleProperty = nameof(Title))]   // TitleProperty -> the H1 heading
24. public class Report
25. {
26.     public string Title { get; set; } = "";
27.     public int Count { get; set; }
28.     [MarkoutSection(Name = "Items")]                    // -> "## Items" heading
29.     public List<Row>? Items { get; set; }              // List<T> -> a table
30. }
31. 
32. [MarkoutSerializable]
33. public class Row { public string Name { get; set; } = ""; public string Value { get; set; } = ""; }
34. 
35. // 2. Register EVERY type on a partial context (the source generator fills it in).
36. [MarkoutContext(typeof(Report))]
37. [MarkoutContext(typeof(Row))]
38. public partial class ReportContext : MarkoutSerializerContext { }
39. 
40. // 3. Serialize THROUGH the context.
41. MarkoutSerializer.Serialize(report, Console.Out, ReportContext.Default);
42. ```

45. 
46. - **No reflection fallback.** There is no `Serialize(obj)` overload. EVERY `MarkoutSerializer.Serialize`
47.   overload takes a `MarkoutSerializerContext` (or `MarkoutTypeInfo<T>`). Skipping the context does
48.   not compile. This is the #1 mistake.
49. - **Register every type.** A model used in output but missing `[MarkoutSerializable]` +
50.   `[MarkoutContext(typeof(T))]` will not serialize. The context class MUST be `partial`.
51. - **Attributes are Markout's, not System.Text.Json's:** `[MarkoutSerializable]` (not
52.   `[JsonSerializable]`), `[MarkoutContext]`, `[MarkoutSection(Name=...)]`, `TitleProperty`,
53.   `[MarkoutPropertyName]`, `[MarkoutIgnore]`. Do not use `Json*` attributes.
54. - **Rendering is driven by type, not markup:** `List<T>` -> table; scalar (`string`/`int`/`bool`) ->
55.   a `Field | Value` row; `[MarkoutSection(Name="X")]` -> a `## X` heading above the property.
56. - **Put `[MarkoutIgnoreInTable]` on non-tabular list properties** (`List<Metric>`, `List<Breakdown>`,
57.   `List<TreeNode>`, `List<Description>`, `Callout`) or they get mistreated as table columns.
58.

60. 
61. `Metric` (bar chart), `Breakdown`/`Slice` (stacked bar), `Callout` (alert), `TreeNode`

73.   `[MarkoutDelta(Delta.Percent)]` on a numeric `Change<V>` appends the signed change, e.g.
74.   `98555 → 61190 (−38%)`; `Delta.Absolute` appends the signed difference; `Delta.Multiple` appends a
75.   multiplicative factor with a direction word, e.g. `15 → 5 (3× fewer)` / `5 → 15 (3× more)` (a zero

80.   `Share`→value; Markdown-only).

99. columns as JSON numbers instead of strings.

102. composite property), structured formatters (TSV/JSONL) **decompose it into typed `{column}_{sub}` columns**

110. Two list-shapes render as multi-format cards from a `[MarkoutSerializable]` model — Markdown table +
111. flat typed JSONL/TSV — with no imperative writer calls:

The pattern is always the same: deserialize your API data, project to a model, serialize. Markout handles the rest. 271. 272. ## Shape Library 273. 274. Each property on a model maps to a data relationship, not a visual element. Renderers decide how to present each shape. 275. 276. | Relationship | C# type | What it means | Markdown | ANSI | 277. |---|---|---|---|---| 278. | **Identity** | `string`, `int`, `bool` | Named value | `Key: value` | Bold key, value | 279. | **Enumeration** | `string[]` | Sequence of items | `- item` | Bullet list | 280. | **Tabulation** | `List` | Uniform records | `\| col \| col \|` | Space-padded table | 281. | **Section** | `[MarkoutSection]` | Logical grouping | `## Heading` | Colored heading | 282. | **Description** | `List` | Terms with explanations | `- **Term:** text` | Bold term, text | 283. | **Measurement** | `List` | Comparative quantities | `Label ████░░ 45` | Colored bars | 284. | **Composition** | `List` | Parts of a whole | `██▓▓▒░` stacked | Colored segments | 285. | **Hierarchy** | `List` | Parent-child structure | `├── node` | Box-drawing tree | 286. | **Quotation** | `CodeSection` | Verbatim content | ` ```code``` ` | Syntax display | 287. | **Attention** | `Callout` | Important messages | `> [!WARNING]` | Colored label | 288. 289. Plus structural shapes: **Quotation** (prose quotation), **Matrix** (2D pivot grid), **Rule** (section separator). 290. 291. ### Record Types 292. 293. Shapes that need structured input provide record types named for what the data *is*, not what it *looks like*: 294. 295. ```csharp 296. new Metric("Build Time", 4.2) // measurement 297. new Description("dotnet-inspect", "API surface inspection tool") // term + explanation 298. new Breakdown("Jan 2025", [new("Critical", 1), new("High", 3)]) // proportional composition 299. new Callout(CalloutSeverity.Warning, "3 vulnerabilities found") // attention 300. new CodeSection("csharp", "public class Foo { }") // verbatim content 301. ``` 302. 303. ## Renderers 304. 305. Markout ships five formatters. The serializer writes through `MarkoutWriter` (the orchestrator) — swap the formatter, change the output. 306. 307. | Formatter | Output | Use case | 308. |---|---|---| 309. | **MarkdownFormatter** | GitHub-Flavored Markdown | Documentation, LLM tool output, rendered reports | 310. | **PlainTextFormatter** | Plain text without markup | Minimal output, no syntax characters | 311. | **UnicodeFormatter** | Box-drawing characters | Rich tables with borders, no color | 312. | **TableFormatter** | Tables, lists, fields | Compact summaries, pretty tables, TSV/JSONL rows | 313. | **DiagramFormatter** | Trees and structural diagrams | Dependency graphs, file trees | 314. 315. Optional packages: 316. 317. | Package | Formatter | Use case | 318. |---|---|---| 319. | **Markout.Ansi.Spectre** | `SpectreFormatter` | Rich terminal UI via Spectre.Console | 320. 321. Formatters declare which shapes they support by implementing capability interfaces (`ITableFormatter`, `IFieldFormatter`, `ITreeFormatter`, etc.). Unsupported shapes are silently skipped — the data is never lost, only the visual sophistication changes. 322. 323. ### Format promises 324. 325. - Markdown table-cell and heading text is treated as literal data: the structural characters `&`, `<`, `>`, and backtick are escaped to entities (`&`, `<`, `>`, ```) so the value renders verbatim rather than being interpreted as HTML or a code span. Table cells additionally normalize the delimiting pipe to `|`. 326. - The exception is content inside a rendered `` span, where those characters are literal: there, a pipe is escaped as `\|` (GFM unescapes it while splitting table rows, before code-span parsing) and angle brackets/ampersands need no escaping. 327. - Semantic inline `...` tags render as Markdown code spans and as plain text in table, TSV, and JSONL output. 328. - `TableFormatter` with `MarkoutTableMode.Tsv` uses stable snake_case headers by default and never emits embedded tabs or newlines in table cells. 329. - `TableFormatter` with `MarkoutTableMode.Jsonl` uses stable snake_case property names by default and emits one JSON object per table row. 330. - `TableFormatter` with `MarkoutTableMode.Pretty` renders the same projection as TSV, with each column starting at a uniform position across rows. 331. 332. ## Templates 333. 334. Templates let you author document structure in Markdown and fill data slots at runtime. The same template renders to any format — Markdown, plain text, or ANSI terminal. 335. 336. **template.md:** 337. 338. ```markdown 339. # .NET Security Report for {{date}} 340. 341. The following vulnerabilities were disclosed this month. 342. 343. {{vuln-table}} 344. 345. | Level | CVSS Range | Response | 346. | ----- | ---------- | -------- | 347. | Critical | 9.0–10.0 | Patch immediately | 348. | High | 7.0–8.9 | Patch within 30 days | 349. 350. {{#if commits}} 351. ## Commits 352. 353. {{commit-table}} 354. {{/if}} 355. ``` 356. 357. **Program.cs:** 358. 359. ```csharp 360. using Markout; 361. using Markout.Templates; 362. 363. var template = MarkoutTemplate.Load("template.md"); 364. template.TableOptions = new TableFormatterOptions(); // smooth column widths 365. 366. template.Bind("date", "February 2026"); 367. template.Bind("vuln-table", vulnerabilityData); // IMarkoutFormattable 368. template.Bind("commits", hasCommits ? "yes" : null); 369. template.Bind("commit-table", commitData); 370. 371. // Markdown output 372. Console.WriteLine(template.Render(new MarkoutWriterOptions { PrettyTables = true })); 373. 374. // Plain text output — same template, different formatter 375. var plainWriter = new MarkoutWriter(Console.Out, new UnicodeFormatter()); 376. template.Render(plainWriter); 377. ``` 378. 379. Templates support: 380. 381. - **`{{key}}`** — inline substitution in headings and prose, or block-level data rendering 382. - **`{{#if key}}`** / **`{{/if}}`** — conditional sections (included when key is bound and non-null) 383. - **Pipe tables** — parsed and re-rendered through the writer's table shape, with optional statistical column-width optimization 384. - **`IMarkoutFormattable`** and **`MarkoutTypeInfo`** bindings for shape-aware data rendering 385. 386. ```bash 387. dotnet add package Markout.Templates 388. ``` 389. 390. ### Template Runner Tool 391. 392. A basic CLI tool is included for rendering templates with string bindings: 393. 394. ```bash 395. dotnet run --project tools/markout-template -- template.md date="February 2026" title="Report" 396. ``` 397. 398. Unbound block placeholders are skipped, so you can render partial templates. Pipe `key=value` lines on stdin for additional bindings. 399. 400. ## Customization Layers 401. 402. Markout provides multiple layers of control, from zero-config to full custom: 403. 404. **Layer 1 — Attributes** (compile-time): Control what's rendered and how. 405. 406. ```csharp 407. [MarkoutPropertyName("Born")] // rename a field 408. [MarkoutSkipNull] // hide when null 409. [MarkoutSection(Name = "Details")] // group into a section 410. [MarkoutDisplayFormat("N0")] // format numbers 411. [MarkoutShowWhen(nameof(HasDetails))] // conditional rendering 412. [MarkoutMaxItems(10)] // truncate long lists 413. [MarkoutSection(FieldOrder = MarkoutFieldOrder.Alphabetical)] // alpha-order field rows 414. [MarkoutValueMap("k=badge", ...)] // map values to badge-prefixed output 415. [MarkoutUnwrap] // inline collection items without section heading 416. [MarkoutIgnoreColumnWhen(...)] // conditionally hide table columns 417. ``` 418. 419. **Layer 2 — Writer Options** (runtime): Control which sections appear. 420. 421. ```csharp 422. var options = new MarkoutWriterOptions 423. { 424. IncludeSections = new HashSet { "Summary", "Errors" }, // only these sections 425. BoldFieldNames = true 426. }; 427. MarkoutSerializer.Serialize(view, Console.Out, new MarkdownFormatter(), context, options); 428. ``` 429. 430. **Layer 3 — Custom Formatter** (code): Implement capability interfaces for custom rendering. 431. 432. ```csharp 433. public class MyFormatter : IMarkoutFormatter, IFieldFormatter, ITableFormatter 434. { 435. // Implement only the interfaces your formatter supports 436. void IFieldFormatter.FormatFieldName(TextWriter w, string key, bool bold) { ... } 437. void ITableFormatter.FormatTable(TextWriter w, ReadOnlySpan headers, IList rows, int skippedRows, MarkoutWriterOptions options) { ... } 438. } 439. ``` 440. 441. ## Installation 442. 443. ```bash 444. dotnet add package Markout 445. ``` 446. 447. The package includes the source generator — no additional packages needed. 448. 449. ## Samples 450. 451. - **[HelloMarkout](samples/HelloMarkout)** — Simplest possible example: a class, a context, one line of serialization 452. - **[RecordDemo](samples/RecordDemo)** — Records as data models 453. - **[GitHubRepo](samples/GitHubRepo)** — GitHub API → fields, breakdowns, metrics, and tables with Spectre, Markdown, table, TSV, and JSONL output 454. - **[GitHubActivity](samples/GitHubActivity)** — User profile and recent events from the GitHub API 455. - **[CanadianContent](samples/CanadianContent)** — Canadian actors and shows with tables, trees, metrics, and multiple renderers 456. - **[LatestCves](samples/LatestCves)** — .NET security advisories with trees and severity breakdowns 457. - **[DotNetReleases](samples/DotNetReleases)** — .NET release information from GitHub 458. - **[Serialization](samples/Serialization)** — Shape gallery, section filtering, and writer API examples 459. - **[TemplateDemo](samples/TemplateDemo)** — Document template with inline tables, conditional sections, and multi-format rendering 460. 461. ## Formats and Agents 462. 463. Agents and LLMs are skilled at two things: using tools and reading text. No single text format is best in all cases — a tool that can produce results in multiple formats is more useful to an agent than one locked to a single output. 464. 465. JSON and Markout are peer options. JSON carries data between systems — APIs, config, round-trip serialization. Markout carries data to readers — humans and agents consuming structured documents. A tool like [dotnet-inspect](https://github.com/richlander/dotnet-inspect) gathers data from NuGet packages, assemblies, and APIs, projects it into Markout models, and offers both `--json` and Markout output. The same section metadata, schema discovery, and projection features enable control and customization upstream of either format generation. 466. 467. Tools that produce a lot of text need standard controls to segment it. Verbosity levels are useful but blunt — they control *how much* without letting you say *which parts*. Markout's section selection (`-s Dependencies`) and column/field projection (`--columns Name,Version`) are sharper instruments, offering the kind of targeted trimming that [Go templates](https://pkg.go.dev/text/template) provide in other ecosystems, but without requiring users to learn a template language. You say what data to keep; the renderer decides how to present it. 468. 469. Tools built on a shared output scheme improve together. When eval sessions reveal that a heading level, table layout, or field ordering works better for agents, a new Markout version carries that improvement to every tool that uses it. 470. 471. ## For Coding Agents 472. 473. If you are an LLM or coding agent building a CLI tool that needs structured, readable output, see **[SKILL.md](SKILL.md)** for step-by-step integration instructions and attribute reference. 474. 475. ## Real-World Usage 476. 477. Markout was created for [dotnet-inspect](https://github.com/richlander/dotnet-inspect), which uses all ten data relationships across 49 models to generate API inspection reports, diff analysis, dependency trees, and security summaries. 478. 479. ## Documentation 480. 481. - **[User Guide](docs/user-guide.md)** — Complete tutorial with attribute reference 482. - **[Shape System Design](docs/design/shape-system.md)** — Data projection model, shape tiers, admission criteria 483. - **[Specification](docs/specification.md)** — Format grammar and type inference rules 484. - **[Nested Lists Guide](docs/nested-lists-guide.md)** — Strategies for nested data structures 485. 486. ## License 487. 488. # Multi-view & verbosity — summary/detail from one model

Real CLIs expose `-v`/`--detail`/`--quiet` and section selectors. The anti-pattern is a separate
render path (or DTO) per level. With Markout you keep **one model** and select what renders — and,
importantly, drive **what you collect** from the requested verbosity so you don't over-scan.

## Compact summary via field layout

`AutoFields` renders scalar properties as fields; tune the summary without new types:

```csharp
[MarkoutSerializable(
    TitleProperty = nameof(Name),
    FieldLayout = FieldLayout.Inline)]   // Table (default) | Inline | Bulleted | Numbered | Plain
public class View
{
    public string Name { get; set; } = "";
    [MarkoutSkipNull] public string? Summary { get; set; }   // drops out of the terse view when null
}
```

`FieldLayout.Inline` gives a pipe-separated one-liner header; `Table` gives a two-column field block.
Choose the terse shape for quiet mode, the fuller sections for detail.

## Verbosity as section selection

Verbosity is a caller concept. Express it as the set of sections to render:

```csharp
static readonly string[] QuietSections  = { "Summary" };
static readonly string[] DetailSections = { "Summary", "Members", "Diagnostics", "Sources" };

var sections = verbose ? DetailSections : QuietSections;
var options = new MarkoutWriterOptions { IncludeSections = new HashSet<string>(sections) };
MarkoutSerializer.Serialize(view, Console.Out, new MarkdownFormatter(), ctx, options);
```

projection* of a section rather than just its presence.

narrow request stays cheap and a `--section Diagnostics` request pulls exactly the data it needs.

in your collection code; Markout only ever sees the populated model + `IncludeSections`.

// Resolve requested sections first, then raise your own verbosity to satisfy them, THEN collect.
Verbosity required = GetRequiredVerbosity(requestedSections);          // e.g. Diagnostics => Detailed
var verbosity = (Verbosity)Math.Max((int)cliVerbosity, (int)required);
var model = Collect(verbosity);                                        // scan only as deep as needed

var options = new MarkoutWriterOptions { IncludeSections = new HashSet<string>(sections) };
MarkoutSerializer.Serialize(model, Console.Out, new MarkdownFormatter(), ctx, options);
```

Markout renders whatever the model carries; the verbosity policy is expressed to it purely through
which properties you populate + `IncludeSections`. This is the pattern behind tools that map
`-D`/`-S` flags to a single reusable view.

# Output formats — one model, many formats

Default `Serialize(...)` emits Markdown. Pass a **formatter** (and optional `MarkoutWriterOptions`)
to get other formats. The anti-pattern is per-format string building (`string.Join("\t", ...)`); let
Markout project the same model to each format so columns/headers stay consistent.

## Formatters

```csharp
MarkoutSerializer.Serialize(r, Console.Out, ctx);                              // Markdown (default)
MarkoutSerializer.Serialize(r, Console.Out, new MarkdownFormatter(), ctx);     // Markdown, explicit
MarkoutSerializer.Serialize(r, Console.Out, new PlainTextFormatter(), ctx);    // plain text / logs (ASCII, no pipes)
MarkoutSerializer.Serialize(r, Console.Out, new UnicodeFormatter(), ctx);      // Unicode box-drawing tables
MarkoutSerializer.Serialize(r, Console.Out, new TableFormatter(), ctx);        // compact pretty rows

using Markout.Ansi.Spectre;                                                    // extra package
MarkoutSerializer.Serialize(r, Console.Out, new SpectreFormatter(AnsiConsole.Console), ctx); // ANSI
```

`Markout.Ansi.Spectre` is a separate NuGet package; Markdown/plain/table/TSV/JSONL need only `Markout`.

## TableFormatter modes + writer options

`TableFormatter` + `MarkoutWriterOptions.TableMode` selects the tabular shape:

```csharp
var opts = new MarkoutWriterOptions
{
    TableMode = MarkoutTableMode.Tsv,          // Pretty | Tsv | Jsonl
    IncludeDescription = false,
    IncludeSections = new HashSet<string> { "Results" },
    JsonTypedValues = true,                    // JSONL/TSV: emit numbers as numbers, not quoted
    MaxItems = 3,                              // cap rows; appends a "... and {N} more" notice
};
MarkoutSerializer.Serialize(report, Console.Out, new TableFormatter(), ctx, opts);
```

- `MarkoutTableMode.Pretty` — columns aligned to a uniform start position.
- `MarkoutTableMode.Tsv` — stable `snake_case` headers; never emits embedded tabs/newlines in cells.
- `MarkoutTableMode.Jsonl` — one record per row (heterogeneous keys; see composite-cells-cards).
- `MaxItems = N` caps EVERY table to N rows and appends `... and {count} more`; works with any formatter,
  so a Markdown view can show the first N rows while TSV/JSONL export them all. (Or per-property:
  `[MarkoutMaxItems(3)]`, with an optional `EllipsisFormat`.)

## Central multi-format dispatch (the CLI `--format` pattern)

Route one model through one method so every command gets every format for free:

```csharp
static void Render<TView, TJson>(TView view, OutputFormat fmt, MarkoutSerializerContext ctx)
{
    switch (fmt)
    {
        case OutputFormat.Text:  MarkoutSerializer.Serialize(view, Console.Out, new PlainTextFormatter(), ctx); break;
        case OutputFormat.Md:    MarkoutSerializer.Serialize(view, Console.Out, new MarkdownFormatter(), ctx,
                                     new MarkoutWriterOptions { MaxItems = 3 }); break;   // first 3 rows + "... and N more"
        case OutputFormat.Table: MarkoutSerializer.Serialize(view, Console.Out, new TableFormatter(), ctx); break;
        case OutputFormat.Tsv:   MarkoutSerializer.Serialize(view, Console.Out, new TableFormatter(), ctx,
                                     new MarkoutWriterOptions { TableMode = MarkoutTableMode.Tsv }); break;
        case OutputFormat.Jsonl: MarkoutSerializer.Serialize(view, Console.Out, new TableFormatter(), ctx,
                                     new MarkoutWriterOptions { TableMode = MarkoutTableMode.Jsonl, JsonTypedValues = true }); break;
    }
}
```

If a format needs byte-exact output (e.g. a verbatim packet), bypass Markout for that one case and
keep Markout for the structured formats — don't try to force it.

## Format promises (rely on these)

- Markdown table cells normalize `|` to `|` (not `\|`).
- TSV uses stable `snake_case` headers and never embeds tabs/newlines in cells.
- Pretty renders the same projection as TSV, aligned.

## Guardrails

- One model → many formats; never hand-assemble TSV/JSONL rows.
- Reach for `IncludeSections`/`IncludeDescription` to trim exports rather than a second model.
- Spectre/ANSI needs the `Markout.Ansi.Spectre` package; the rest do not.
